title: Another self
hookLine: Aristotle: a friend is another self (Nicomachean Ethics 9.4)

cards: Good news arrives, and some people's thumbs go straight to one particular name. Bad news, the same name. Nobody decided that on purpose; it just grew.
In the ninth book of his Ethics, Aristotle looks at that kind of bond and asks an odd question: where does it come from?
His answer starts somewhere unexpected, not with the friend at all, but with how a good person lives with themself.

teach.b: First, the marks of a friend.

Aristotle lists what people take friendship to mean: wishing good to someone for their sake, wishing them to exist and to live, spending time with them, choosing the same things, sharing their griefs and their joys.

Second, it starts at home. Then he turns the list around. A good person already relates to themself this way: wants their own good, wants to go on living, is glad of their own company, and isn't at war inside.
And so, he says, the good person is to a friend as to themself, for a friend is another self: in Greek, two words, allos autos. Not a copy.
Someone whose good matters to you the way your own does, whose griefs land on you as if they were yours.
He then draws bad people as the opposite: at odds with themselves, running from their own company, full of regret for what they've chosen, with no friendly feeling even toward themselves.
Some readers take a hopeful thought from the passage: peace inside and friendship outside may grow from the same root, and tending one may help the other.

how: Aristotle's idea of the friend as another self, from book nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, is studied in philosophy courses, and some readers use it to reflect on how they treat friends and themselves.

o: a friend who thinks and acts exactly like you
the hidden self you show to nobody else
a friend whose good matters to you like your own

games.q: Aristotle on friendship — tap the pairs.

s: Aristotle means a friend should be a copy of you
another self means someone whose good matters to you like your own.
sharing griefs and joys is on Aristotle's list of friendship's marks
along with wishing their good and spending time together.
Aristotle says how you live with yourself has nothing to do with friendship
he starts with a good person's relation to themself.

games.q: you're Aristotle, explaining where friendship comes from. where do you look first?
o: at how a good person relates to themself.
at what a friend can do for you.
at how many friends a person has.
games.why: he looks inward first: a good person already wishes their own good and enjoys their own company, and is to a friend as to themself.

practice: Bring one friend to mind and, breathing in, wish them what you'd wish yourself today: rest, a good meal, an easy hour, some good news.

Breathing out, if it isn't too hard, wish yourself the same, and go back and forth, friend and self, until the two wishes start to sound alike. If one comes easily and the other is hard, just notice which, without judging it.

wordCard.voice: Another self. Aristotle's phrase, allos autos: a friend is someone whose good matters to you the way your own does. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: another self, Aristotle's phrase for a friend.

carryVoice: Your line: isn't at war inside. Peace at home, and a friend as another self. Rest well.
